warmup.q: The payments app splits its payments over 32 computers by payment number. Each computer keeps an index on card that covers only its own payments. The fraud check asks for every payment card F made today. How many computers does it have to ask?
options: 1: the index says where to look
As many as card F has payments
None: a list kept on the side answers it
warmup.why: Each computer's index covers only its own payments, and card F's payments were placed by payment number, so any of the 32 may hold one, and no computer's index knows what the others hold. The check has to ask all 32 and put the answers together, even when card F has no payments at all. "As many as it has payments" is how the second kind of index in this lesson behaves: all of card F's entries sit in one place, and they point at the computers that hold the payments.

sections.h: Each shard indexes its own payments, so a search by card asks them all
sections.html:
Every card payment passes the fraud check from the opening: how many payments has this card made in the last 60 seconds?

On one computer, the app would answer with an index, a lookup table from a value to where its records live. The payments sit in a table, a list of records with the same fields, like the rows of a spreadsheet, and each field, such as the card, is a column. With an index on the card column, the app finds card F's payments in one step instead of reading every row. (It indexes a code worked out from the card number, the card fingerprint.)

But our payments no longer fit on one computer. They're split over 8 computers, and each piece of the data, on its own computer, is a shard. A payment's shard comes from its payment number. The app runs the number through a hash function, a fixed recipe that turns any text into a number that looks random, and takes the remainder after dividing by 8. The value that picks the shard is the partition key. Finding a payment by its number asks exactly one shard.

The fraud check doesn't have a payment number, though. It has a card. An index on a column that isn't the partition key is a secondary index. With shards, we have to decide where its entries live.

Picture a city library with eight branches. Each book sits at one branch, picked by its number, and each branch keeps a catalogue of its own books only. Adding a book is easy: the branch that gets it files the card. But to find every book by one author, you phone all eight branches and wait for each librarian to look.

The simplest index for our shards works the same way. The branch is a shard, a book is a payment and the branch's catalogue is that shard's index. Shard 2's index maps card F to the payments of card F stored on shard 2, and to nothing else. This is a local index, also called document-partitioned, because it's split exactly like the records (documents) it points to.

Writes stay simple. A payment and its index entry go to the same shard, in one local transaction, a group of changes that happen all together or not at all. So the index is never behind its payments.

Reads by card pay for it. Card F's payments were placed by payment number, so they can be on any shard, and shard 2's index knows nothing about shard 5. The check has to ask every shard and merge the answers, which is called a scatter-gather read. In the Try it below, card-242's 10 payments sit on 6 of the 8 shards, and the check asks all 8. A card with no payments still asks all 8, because no shard can tell that the others have nothing.

The cost grows with the shard count. At 2,000 checks a second, that's 16,000 shard requests a second on 8 shards, and 64,000 on 32. Adding shards adds no capacity for this question: every new shard receives all 2,000 checks a second, like the old ones.

A local index can't keep a value unique, either. No shard sees the others' entries, so none can tell that a value is already used elsewhere. MongoDB, a popular database program that can split its data over shards, says so in its manual: on a split collection (its word for a table), a unique index works only if it is the shard key (its name for the partition key) or starts with it.

None of this hurts when the question also names the partition key. If the payments were split by shop instead, "card F's payments at shop M-0042" would go to that shop's shard and use the local index there. A local index is cheap when a question names the partition key, and costly when it doesn't.

Asking 8 shards costs 8 times the work. It also costs time, in a way that surprises most people. Next, we'll measure it.

try.title: Count the shards a fraud check asks
steps: Read ShardsContactedDemo.kt. It splits 10,000 made-up payments from 1,000 cards over 8, and then 32, shards by payment number. Then it counts the shards each lookup asks: by payment number, by card through a local index, and by card through a global index, an index split by card that the third section builds.
Predict: going from 8 to 32 shards, what happens to the cost of 2,000 fraud checks a second with each index?
Run it from the labs folder. It needs no Docker.

code.title: ShardsContactedDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.shard.l04.demo import java.nio.ByteBuffer import java.security.MessageDigest fun shardFor(key: String, shards: Int): Int = Math.floorMod(ByteBuffer.wrap(MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5").digest(key.toByteArray())).long, shards.toLong()).toInt() /** 10,000 payments over 1,000 cards, sharded by payment id. The fraud check asks: what has card-242 done? */ fun main() { val payments = (0 until 10_000).map { "pay-$it" to "card-${it % 1_000}" } for (shards in listOf(8, 32)) { val rowShard = payments.associate { (id, _) -> id to shardFor(id, shards) } val card242 = payments.filter { it.second == "card-242" }.map { it.first } println("$shards shards; card-242 has ${card242.size} payments, on shards ${card242.map { rowShard.getValue(it) }.sorted()}") println(" find pay-1234 by id: asks 1 shard") // local index: each shard indexes its own rows, so all of them must be asked println(" find by card, local index: asks $shards shards; each payment writes 1 shard") // global index: all of card-242's entries sit on one index shard, then fetch the rows val rowShards = card242.map { rowShard.getValue(it) }.toSet().size println(" find by card, global index: asks 1 index shard + $rowShards row shards; each payment writes 2 shards") println(" 2,000 fraud checks a second cost ${"%,d".format(2_000 * shards)} shard requests with the local index, ${"%,d".format(2_000 * (1 + rowShards))} with the global one") } }

try.expect:
8 shards; card-242 has 10 payments, on shards [0, 1, 1, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 7, 7]
  find pay-1234 by id:            asks 1 shard
  find by card, local index:      asks 8 shards; each payment writes 1 shard
  find by card, global index:     asks 1 index shard + 6 row shards; each payment writes 2 shards
  2,000 fraud checks a second cost 16,000 shard requests with the local index, 14,000 with the global one
32 shards; card-242 has 10 payments, on shards [0, 1, 4, 5, 15, 17, 19, 20, 23, 28]
  find pay-1234 by id:            asks 1 shard
  find by card, local index:      asks 32 shards; each payment writes 1 shard
  find by card, global index:     asks 1 index shard + 10 row shards; each payment writes 2 shards
  2,000 fraud checks a second cost 64,000 shard requests with the local index, 22,000 with the global one

The local index's read cost is the number of shards, so it grows four times from 8 to 32. The global index asks one index shard plus the shards that hold the card's payments. That depends on how many payments the card has, not on the number of shards (at most 11 here). If the index also stored the columns the check needs, it would ask 1 shard. Writes go the other way: 1 shard for the local index, 2 for the global one.

aside.title: Why not keep the whole index on one extra machine?
aside.html: You could, and the fraud check would ask that one machine. But every payment, on every shard, would then send an index entry to it, so it would take the index writes of the whole app. When it slows down, every payment waits on it, and when it fails, nobody can look anything up by card. That's the one-machine limit that splitting the data was meant to remove. The third section keeps the idea and splits that index machine into shards of its own.

sections.h: Asking every shard means waiting for the slowest one
sections.html:
A scatter-gather read is done when the last shard answers. How long a query, a question sent to the data, takes then depends on more than the average shard.

Latency is the time a request takes. Latency, percentiles and the tail, in the first track, showed how to describe it. Sort the times of many requests. The p99, or 99th percentile, is the time that 99 requests in 100 beat, and the p50, or median, is the time in the middle. The slow requests at the end of the list are called the tail.

Let's model a shard. The demo below draws made-up but typical reply times: 2 to 3 ms (thousandths of a second) most of the time, but 1 reply in 100 takes 50 ms. Real machines have such moments, such as a pause to clean up memory or a disk busy with background work. Asking one shard, the p99 is 3.0 ms, because the slow replies hide in the last 1%.

Now ask 10 shards and wait for all of them. The query is fast only if all 10 replies are fast. The chance of that is 0.99 multiplied by itself 10 times, written 0.99^10, about 0.904. So 1 - 0.99^10, about 9.6% of queries, wait for at least one slow reply. The demo measured 9.7%. For 50 shards it's 39.5%, and for 100 it's 63%. At 100 shards, more than half of all queries take 50 ms, so even the median is 50 ms. Here the library picture breaks down: eight phone calls sound fine, but a query to 100 shards waits for the slowest of 100 machines, every time.

At 10 shards, each shard's p99 becomes the query's p90, the time that 90 queries in 100 beat.

Every product with local indexes has this shape underneath, with a few tricks on top.

MongoDB puts a router program called mongos in front of its shards. It sends a query that names the shard key only to the shards that own that key, and any other query to every shard of the collection. Each shard picks its own best index, and mongos merges the results. It even passes a limit (at most 10 results, say) to every shard, then applies it again to the merged answer.

Cassandra, a database program that spreads data over a cluster of equal machines called nodes (Inside a Cassandra cluster, two lessons on, opens it up), keeps local indexes too. In Cassandra 5.0 they're called Storage-Attached Indexes (SAI). A query on SAI columns without a partition key reads the cluster in rounds. The node handling it asks a few slices of the data at once, guesses from the rows that come back how many more slices it needs, and stops as soon as it has the number of rows the query asked for (its LIMIT). A query whose matches are rare visits most of the cluster. Name the partition key as well, and it reads one partition, the rows that share that key.

OpenSearch and Elasticsearch, two closely related search engines that find documents by the words in them, are the extreme case. Each shard keeps an inverted index, a map from each word to the documents that contain it, over its own documents only. (Indexes for text, time and vectors, in the Storage engines track, built one.) Each shard is kept as two or more copies, called replicas, on different machines, and a search goes to one copy of every shard. Each copy returns its best hits, one machine merges them, and then it fetches the winning documents. You can also have OpenSearch pick the shard from a value you choose, such as the shop. With this custom routing, documents that share the value live on one shard, and a search that passes it asks only that shard.

The cure for the tail is the same in all of them: ask fewer shards. Include the partition key, route by it, or keep the shard count no larger than the data needs. Hedged requests help too. If a shard hasn't answered after a short wait, send the same read to another copy of that shard and take whichever answers first.

All of these keep the index next to its rows. Next, we'll turn the index around and keep each card's entries in one place.

try.title: Measure the tail as a query asks more shards
steps: Read FanOutTailDemo.kt. One shard answers in 2 to 3 ms, but 1 time in 100 it takes 50 ms. A query that asks N shards takes as long as the slowest of N such replies. The demo runs 20,000 queries for each N. It never really waits: a random number generator with a fixed seed draws each reply time, so every run prints the same table.
Predict the p99 for 1 shard and for 10, and the number of shards at which the median becomes 50 ms.

code.title: FanOutTailDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.shard.l04.demo import java.util.Random /** Each shard answers in 2 to 3 ms, except 1 time in 100 it takes 50 ms. A scatter-gather waits for the slowest. */ fun main() { val rnd = Random(42) fun shardMillis() = if (rnd.nextInt(100) == 0) 50.0 else 2.0 + rnd.nextDouble() fun pct(sorted: List<Double>, p: Double) = sorted[maxOf(0, Math.ceil(p / 100 * sorted.size).toInt() - 1)] println("shards asked p50 ms p90 ms p99 ms queries over 10 ms 1 - 0.99^shards") for (shards in listOf(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100)) { val q = List(20_000) { (1..shards).maxOf { shardMillis() } }.sorted() val slow = q.count { it > 10.0 } / 200.0 println("%12d %6.1f %6.1f %6.1f %17.1f%% %14.1f%%".format( shards, pct(q, 50.0), pct(q, 90.0), pct(q, 99.0), slow, (1 - Math.pow(0.99, shards.toDouble())) * 100)) } }

try.expect:
shards asked   p50 ms   p90 ms   p99 ms   queries over 10 ms   1 - 0.99^shards
           1      2.5      2.9      3.0                 0.9%              1.0%
           2      2.7      3.0     50.0                 2.1%              2.0%
           5      2.9      3.0     50.0                 4.9%              4.9%
          10      2.9      3.0     50.0                 9.7%              9.6%
          20      3.0     50.0     50.0                18.1%             18.2%
          50      3.0     50.0     50.0                39.5%             39.5%
         100     50.0     50.0     50.0                63.0%             63.4%

The measured share of slow queries follows 1 - 0.99^N closely. The p99 jumps to 50 ms as soon as a query asks two shards, and the p90 at 20. At 100 shards more than half of all queries wait for a slow reply, so the median is 50 ms. Nothing about any single shard changed, only how many each query waits for.

sections.h: One index split by card: one shard to ask, and an answer that can be late
sections.html:
Go back to the library. Instead of eight small catalogues, it keeps one big one, split by the author's surname: A to F at branch 1, G to M at branch 2, and so on. To find every book by Fowler, you phone branch 1 once, get the full list, and then fetch each book from wherever it sits.

That's a global index: one index over all the payments, itself split into shards by the value it indexes. All of card F's entries go to the index shard picked by hashing F, whichever shards the payments live on. Its other name is term-partitioned: split by the term, the indexed value. A lookup by card asks one index shard, which returns payment numbers, and then fetches those payments from their shards. In the first Try it, that was 1 index shard plus 6 row shards, the shards holding card-242's 10 payments, and 1 shard for a card with none. If the index also keeps a copy of the columns the check needs, there's no fetch at all, and the lookup asks exactly one shard. DynamoDB calls those copied columns projected attributes.

The cost moves to writes. When branch 5 buys a book by Fowler, it has to post a catalogue card to branch 1. A new payment lands on its own shard, and its index entry lands on its card's index shard, usually another machine. Each indexed column adds one more shard to every write. A change to an indexed value touches two entries: the old one is deleted and the new one added. Keeping a payment and its entries in step across machines leaves two choices.

The first is one distributed transaction per write: a transaction whose changes span several machines and still happen all together or not at all. CockroachDB, TiDB and YugabyteDB, databases that speak SQL (the common language for asking databases questions) and spread their tables over many machines, work this way. Each index is stored as its own range of keys, split and placed like table data, and its entries are written in the same transaction as the row. The index is never behind its rows, and it can keep a value unique. Each write pays for the machines agreeing that the transaction is final, which Atomic commit across machines, in the Transactions track, takes apart.

The second is to update the index asynchronously: the write is confirmed first, and the index entry follows a little later. DynamoDB, Amazon's database service that you rent instead of running it yourself, does this for its global secondary indexes (GSIs). DynamoDB calls its shards partitions. Its docs say changes reach a GSI "within a fraction of a second, under normal conditions", and later in rare failures. A GSI can only be read with eventual consistency, a promise that a read may return an old answer for a while but catches up once writes stop. So a read through the index can miss a write that has already succeeded, like a Fowler book on the shelf at branch 5 while its card is still in the post. The stepper walks through one, and the Try it measures how often a check 50 ms after each payment misses it. If the app must see its own new payment, it reads that payment by its key from the main table instead.

An asynchronous index has a second effect. A GSI has partitions of its own, chosen by its own key. If the GSI can't keep up with its updates, DynamoDB throttles writes to the main table, slowing or refusing them on purpose, even when the table itself has room. An index on a column with few values, such as status, sends the entry of every PENDING payment to one GSI partition, and the refusal names the cause: IndexWriteKeyRangeThroughputExceeded. A hot key, one key that gets far more traffic than the rest, is still a hot key inside an index, as Partitioning: consistent hashing and hot keys showed for tables.

DynamoDB has local secondary indexes (LSIs) as well. An LSI keeps the table's partition key and sorts each partition's items (DynamoDB's word for records) by another column, and it's stored with that partition. Because it lives with its rows, it can be read with strong consistency: a read that always sees the latest confirmed write. That's the whole trade in one product. A local index stays in step but needs the partition key; a global index finds any value on one shard, but may lag.

Two indexes, opposite strengths. Next, we'll choose between them, one question at a time.

frames.say: The row shard sends the index entry, F: pay-9001, toward index shard 1 asynchronously, so it waits in a queue. In this model it lands 120 ms later. DynamoDB only promises a fraction of a second under normal conditions, and longer when something is failing.

frames.say: 50 ms later card F pays again, and the fraud check runs: how many payments did F make in the last minute? It reads index shard 1 and gets three. pay-9001 is missing, though it was saved 50 ms ago. Nothing is broken. This is what asynchronous means: a stale read, an answer from before the newest write.

frames.say: At the same moment, a read of pay-9001 by its payment number goes to row shard 2 and finds it. Reads by the partition key see every confirmed write; reads through the global index may not. That gap is the whole trade.

frames.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 324" role="img" aria-label="At 120 ms the queued entry lands on index shard 1"><defs><marker id="arr" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse"><path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" class="ln"/></marker></defs><text class="t t-a" x="16" y="26" text-anchor="start">t = 120 ms</text><rect class="box" x="16" y="120" width="150" height="60" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="91.0" y="146.0" text-anchor="middle">payment service</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="91.0" y="164.0" text-anchor="middle">and fraud check</text><rect class="box" x="260" y="30" width="190" height="66" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="355.0" y="59.0" text-anchor="middle">row shard 2</text><text class="t-s t-code" x="355.0" y="77.0" text-anchor="middle">pay-9001, card F</text><rect class="box" x="260" y="214" width="190" height="66" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="355.0" y="243.0" text-anchor="middle">index update queue</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="355.0" y="261.0" text-anchor="middle">empty</text><rect class="box-a" x="480" y="120" width="204" height="76" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="582.0" y="145.0" text-anchor="middle">index shard 1</text><text class="t-s t-code" x="582.0" y="163.0" text-anchor="middle">F: pay-12 pay-31 pay-77</text><text class="t-s t-a" x="582.0" y="181.0" text-anchor="middle">+ pay-9001</text><line class="ln-a" x1="450" y1="240" x2="478" y2="194" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><text class="t-s t-m" x="350" y="312" text-anchor="middle">the entry lands; the index has caught up</text></svg>
frames.say: At 120 ms the entry lands on index shard 1. From now on a lookup by card F returns four payments. If the index shard were overloaded, the queue would grow, and DynamoDB would start refusing writes to the main table so the index can't fall further behind.

frames.say: A check at 150 ms sees all four, from one index shard. One shard per lookup is why you'd build a global index; the window between 0 and 120 ms is what it costs. A thief's program that fires payments 50 ms apart lives entirely inside that window.

try.title: How often does the fraud check miss the newest payment?
steps: Read StaleIndexDemo.kt. It's a model that runs on pretend time. Each index entry lands 30 to 120 ms after its payment, and 1 time in 50 it takes 600 ms, as if the index shard were busy. Those delays are made up, because DynamoDB doesn't publish real ones. The fraud check reads the index some time after each payment.
Predict the share of checks that miss the payment when the check runs 50 ms after it.
Run it from the labs folder. Then change the 600 to 2,000, run it again and see which line moves.

code.title: StaleIndexDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.shard.l04.demo import java.util.Random /** * A model of an asynchronous global index, on virtual time. Each index entry lands some time after its * row: here 30 to 120 ms, and 1 time in 50 it takes 600 ms (a busy index shard). These lags are made * up for the model; DynamoDB only promises "a fraction of a second, under normal conditions". * The fraud check reads the index some milliseconds after each payment. How often is it missing? */ fun main() { val rnd = Random(7) val lags = List(10_000) { if (rnd.nextInt(50) == 0) 600L else 30L + rnd.nextInt(91) } println("check runs after index still missing the payment") for (after in listOf(10L, 50L, 100L, 250L, 1_000L)) { val missing = lags.count { it > after } println("%13d ms %,6d of 10,000 (%.1f%%)".format(after, missing, missing / 100.0)) } println("reading the row by its key: 0 of 10,000 missing, at any time") }

try.expect:
check runs after   index still missing the payment
           10 ms   10,000 of 10,000 (100.0%)
           50 ms    7,694 of 10,000 (76.9%)
          100 ms    2,316 of 10,000 (23.2%)
          250 ms      206 of 10,000 (2.1%)
         1000 ms        0 of 10,000 (0.0%)
reading the row by its key: 0 of 10,000 missing, at any time

With these delays, a check 50 ms after a payment misses it three times in four, and even at 250 ms the rare slow update still causes 2.1% misses. With 2,000 instead of 600, the 1,000 ms line goes from 0 to about 2%: the rare slow update decides how long you have to wait to be sure. Reads by the payment number are never stale, because they go to the shard that took the write.

sections.h: Choosing an index for each question the app asks
sections.html:
Every difference between the two designs follows from one fact: where the index entries live.

Local index (document-partitioned) Global index (term-partitioned)
Entries live with their rows, on every shard on index shards picked by the indexed value
A write touches its own shard its own shard, plus one index shard per indexed column
A lookup by the value asks every shard, or one if it also names the partition key 1 index shard, plus the shards holding the rows unless their columns are copied in
Behind its rows? never never with a distributed transaction (CockroachDB, TiDB); sometimes when asynchronous (DynamoDB GSI)
Unique values only if the index includes the partition key yes, with a transactional index
Examples MongoDB, Cassandra SAI, OpenSearch, DynamoDB LSI DynamoDB GSI, CockroachDB, TiDB, YugabyteDB

For every lookup that doesn't use the partition key, ask three things. How often does it run? How many shards will a scatter-gather ask, now and after the next two rounds of growth? And must it see a write that finished a moment ago?

Let's ask them of the app's two lookups by card. The first is a screen for the company's fraud analysts, the people who look into odd cards by hand: "card F's payments this month". It runs a few times a minute, and a second of lag doesn't matter. A GSI is a fine choice, and so is a local index on 8 shards.

The second is the fraud check from the opening, which runs while the card reader waits. It runs 2,000 times a second, must answer within 20 ms, and must count the payment from 50 ms ago, because a thief's program can fire payments that fast. Say the app has grown to 64 shards. A local index fails the time limit: 1 - 0.99^64 is 47%, so nearly half the checks wait on a slow shard. A GSI fails the freshness test. Neither index fits.

The answer is a separate table, split by card, that holds a velocity counter: how many payments each card made in the last minute. The payment itself updates the counter, in the same request, on the card's own shard, so the next check always sees it. That's a hand-made global index, kept in step by the code that writes it. The worked example builds it.

Hand-made indexes have one known failure: drift. If the app saves the payment and then crashes before it updates the counter, the two disagree, and nothing repairs them. Keep the two writes in one transaction where the store allows it (DynamoDB transactions cover up to 100 items). Or build the second table from the first table's change stream, a feed of every change made to it, which the Stream processing track builds.

Choose the index per question, not per table.

Neither kind is free, and that's the limit of everything in this lesson. A local index pays on every read, a global index pays on every write and may lag, and a hand-made one pays in code you have to keep correct. We can only choose where the cost lands.

opening:
Picture a thief with a stolen card number. A program tests it with small payments at online shops, one every 50 milliseconds.

The coffee-shop payments app has a guard for this. Before it says yes, it counts the card's payments in the last minute and refuses when there are more than five. On one computer, an index on the card answers that in a millisecond. But the app's payments now live on 8 computers, split by payment number, so card F's payments could be on any of them. The team adds computers to go faster, and the check gets slower.

It's easy to expect an index to work the same on 8 machines as on one, because on one machine there's only one place to put it. With 8, you have to choose.

In Rebalancing and request routing, we found a payment's shard from its payment number. In this lesson, we'll look payments up by something else, build two kinds of index, and catch one answering from the past. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a thief testing a stolen card, and a fraud check that slowed down as the app grew. A local index asks every shard and waits for the slowest. A global index asks one, but can answer from before the newest payment. The check that needed both got its own table, split by card.

Next time you search your order history in a shopping app, ask what it's searching by. If a brand-new order is missing for a second, you've probably met an asynchronous index.

Next, we'll open up Cassandra, a database where no machine is in charge, and find out how each machine knows where every key lives and which machines are alive.

worked.title: Design the fraud check that counts a card's recent payments

steps.say: Write down what the check needs, with numbers. It runs while the card reader waits for a yes, so its time limit is part of that wait. The p99 is the time 99 checks in 100 must beat.
steps.code:
checks             2,000 / s at peak
question           how many payments has card F made in the last 60 s?
budget             20 ms at p99
must see           a payment from 50 ms ago (a thief's program fires that fast)
payments table     hash-sharded by payment id, 64 shards
one shard          2 to 3 ms, 1 reply in 100 takes 50 ms

steps.say: Option A, a local index on card. Every check asks every shard. Work out the load and the tail before trying it.
steps.code: val shards = 64 val shardRequests = 2_000 * shards // 128,000 a second, for one query type val slow = 1 - Math.pow(0.99, shards.toDouble()) // 0.47: 47% of checks wait on a 50 ms reply // p99 = 50 ms against a 20 ms budget: rejected

steps.say: Option B, a GSI on card. Each check asks one index shard, so the load and the tail are fine. But a payment's entry lands some time after the payment: a fraction of a second normally, longer when something fails. The thief's second payment, 50 ms after the first, is checked against an index that may not have the first yet. Rejected for this check; keep it for the analysts' screen.
steps.code:
requests per check   1 index shard (attributes projected)
fresh?               no: GSI reads are eventually consistent
verdict              fine for the analysts' screen, wrong for the card reader's check

steps.say: Option C, a table split by card, updated by the payment itself. Count and add happen on the card's own shard, in one request, so the next check always sees the new count. Old minute buckets expire by themselves after a set time (DynamoDB calls this TTL, time to live).
steps.code: // partition key: card fingerprint; one item per card per minute bucket suspend fun velocity(card: String, now: Instant): Long { val bucket = now.epochSecond / 60 // one conditional update on ONE shard: add 1 and return the new count, atomically return store.increment(key = "VEL#$card#$bucket", by = 1, ttlSeconds = 120) } // in the payment request: refuse when the card exceeds its limit if (velocity(card, clock.instant()) > 5) decline("velocity")

steps.say: Check what C costs. It's one more write per payment, on the card's shard. A card used very often is a hot key, so a test card hammered by a thief's program lands on one partition. Here that's what you want: it's the card you're about to block. The payment and the counter are two items, so put them in one transaction, or accept that a crash between them undercounts by one.
steps.code:
A local index   B GSI          C velocity table
shards per check    64              1              1
p99 within 20 ms    no              yes            yes
sees 50 ms ago      yes             not always     yes
extra write         none            1 (async)      1 (sync, same request)

lab.title: Build a local and a global index, and catch a stale read
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. They need no Docker. All 7 fail with NotImplementedError. Time in the tests is a VirtualClock, a pretend clock: nothing happens between two calls to advance, so every check of how stale the index is comes out exact.
In Indexes.kt, write LocalIndexTable.insert and findByCard. The two local-index tests pass: one write touches 1 shard, and one lookup asks all 8, even for a card nobody used.

Write GlobalIndexTable.insert, which stores the payment now and queues its index entry for clock.now + lagMillis. Then write findByCard, which first applies every entry whose time has come. The test with a 200 ms delay checks that the index misses the payment at 100 ms and has it at 200 ms.

Experiment: in the test a fraud check 50 ms after each payment..., change the delay of 20 to 50, then to 51. At 50 the check still sees every payment, because an entry due at the check's own moment is applied first. At 51 it misses every one. Then put it back.
hints: GlobalIndexTable.insert: pending += Pending(clock.now + lagMillis, seq++, p.card, p.id). The seq keeps entries with the same due time in the order they were written.

GlobalIndexTable.findByCard: while (pending.isNotEmpty() && pending.peek().dueAt <= clock.now), take the entry with poll() and add it to index[indexShardOf(e.card)]. Then shardsContacted = 1 + ids.map(::shardOf).toSet().size.

drill.title: Both lookups from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the lookup by card for a local index (localIndex: List<Map<String, Set<String>>>, one map per shard) and for a global index (globalIndex: List<Map<String, Set<String>>>, one map per index shard, picked by shardFor(card, n)). Each returns the payment ids it found and the number of shards it asked. Then say in one sentence what the global version needs on every write that the local one doesn't.

answer.html: fun findLocal(localIndex: List<Map<String, Set<String>>>, card: String): Pair<Set<String>, Int> = // every shard may hold some of the card's rows: ask them all localIndex.flatMap { it[card].orEmpty() }.toSet() to localIndex.size fun findGlobal(globalIndex: List<Map<String, Set<String>>>, card: String, rowShardOf: (String) -> Int): Pair<Set<String>, Int> { // one index shard holds every entry for this card val ids = globalIndex[shardFor(card, globalIndex.size)][card].orEmpty() return ids to 1 + ids.map(rowShardOf).toSet().size // plus the shards that hold the rows } // A global index needs a second write, to another machine, for every indexed column of every row: // either in a distributed transaction or asynchronously, and then reads through it can be stale.

recap: A secondary index on split data lives in one of two places: next to its rows on every shard (a local, or document-partitioned, index) or split into shards of its own by the indexed value (a global, or term-partitioned, index).
A local index costs one shard per write and every shard per lookup, unless the lookup also names the partition key. It can't keep a value unique across shards.
A scatter-gather read is as slow as its slowest shard. If 1 reply in 100 is slow, 1 - 0.99^N of queries are slow: 9.6% at 10 shards. More shards add no capacity for such a question.

A global index answers from one index shard, but each write needs a second machine: in a distributed transaction (CockroachDB, TiDB, YugabyteDB) or asynchronously (DynamoDB's GSIs). An asynchronous index can miss a write that already succeeded, and a GSI that can't keep up slows writes to its table.
Choose per question: how often it runs, how many shards it asks, and how fresh it must be. When neither index fits, build a table split by the value and update it with the write.
The limit: no index is free. A local one pays on reads, a global one on writes and freshness, a hand-made one in code that can drift out of step.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to add a DynamoDB GSI on card fingerprint and use it for the fraud check that counts a card's payments while the card reader waits. Explain what the GSI gives, what it doesn't, and what you'd do instead.
explain.answer: A GSI is a second copy of the data, split by card fingerprint instead of payment number, so all of one card's entries sit on one index partition. A lookup by card is one request to one partition, and if the needed columns are copied into the index, it never touches the main table. That's far better than asking every partition. What it doesn't give is freshness. DynamoDB updates a GSI asynchronously, usually within a fraction of a second, and reads from it are only eventually consistent. A thief's program that fires payments 50 ms apart can get its second and third payments checked against an index that doesn't have the first yet, which is exactly the case the check exists for. The GSI also adds writes on partitions of its own, and if those can't keep up, DynamoDB slows the payments table itself. Instead I'd keep a small table split by card, one item per card per minute, and add one to it in the payment request itself, so the next check on that card always sees it. I'd keep the GSI for the analysts' screen, where a second of lag doesn't matter.

deeper.html:
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 7, explains a cost of global (term-partitioned) indexes that this lesson skipped. A question with two conditions, say card F and shop M-0042, finds each condition's matches on a different index shard. The two lists of matches then have to travel across the network and be compared. Search engines spend a lot of engineering on exactly that.

Cassandra's Storage-Attached Indexes index each node's data as it's written: the table it keeps in memory (the memtable) and the sorted files it writes to disk (SSTables, from LSM trees, SSTables and Bloom filters in the Storage engines track). They take a fraction of the disk space of Cassandra's older secondary indexes, and one query can use several of them.

Hand-made indexes are common in Cassandra, where the usual advice is one table per question. Cassandra's materialized views were meant to keep such tables up to date for you, but they've been marked experimental since 4.0, so most teams write both tables from the app, or from a change stream. The book points out that hand-made indexes drift when a write reaches one table and not the other.

DynamoDB keeps adding to GSIs. Since November 2025 a GSI key can combine up to four attributes for the partition key and four for the sort key, so you no longer glue keys together by hand, like MERCH#M-0042#FAILED. Its global tables, copies of one table in several regions of the world, can be set up to give strongly consistent reads across regions; those allow GSIs (still eventually consistent) but not LSIs.

OpenSearch decides which copy of each shard a search goes to by adaptive replica selection: it prefers copies that answered recent requests quickly and have short queues of waiting searches. That's a built-in way of steering around the slow copy that sets a scatter-gather's tail.

Elastic's advice on shard sizes follows from the scatter-gather picture too. Each shard runs its part of a search on one thread, one path of work inside the program, so too many small shards use up the threads kept for searching.
